etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 人 (hito, “person”) + 質 (shichi, “pawn, hock”). The shichi changes to jichi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
The original sense was “indentureship”, from the sense of a person being as if in pawn until a debt is paid. The “hostage” sense then arose by extension, from the person being in pawn until a ransom is paid or some other condition is met.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: This form is likely a back-formation from from 余(よ)っ程(ぽど) (yoppodo), interpreting the geminated consonant as an intensifier. Ultimately from よき (yoki, “good”) + ほど (hodo, “extent”). The use of the character 余 is an example of ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)).

A bound form only appearing in compounds. Compare the formation of 目 (ma, bound form in compounds) and 目 (me, standalone form), 手 (ta, bound form in compounds) and 手 (te, standalone form).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 義理 (MC ngjeH liX).
Originally, in Middle Chinese and early Japanese attestations, the term carried a philosophical and textual meaning of “righteous principle”, “reason”, or “significance”. During the Muromachi and Edo periods, under the influence of a stratified feudal society, samurai ethics, and the merchant class, the concept underwent semantic narrowing in Japan. The “correct path” shifted to refer specifically to the reciprocal behavioral norms, social debts, and favors expected between individuals in a hierarchical community. This transformed the philosophical concept into a localized social contract and “burden of obligation”, famously contrasting with 人情 (ninjō, “human feeling”). This specialized sense developed entirely internally within Japan.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese verb 老ゆ (oyu).
Development
Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 上(かみ)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 革命 (MC keak mjaengH, “to switch to a new dynasty/regime”). This word has been used for a long time in Japan, starting from the introduction of I Ching (易經). Fukuzawa Yukichi (福󠄁澤 諭󠄀吉), in Western Affairs (『西洋事情』, 1866–1870), used this word as a translation of the English word "revolution", and it was later popularised by Nakae Chōmin (中江 兆民) and others.
